result: The other day, I watched a bumblebee land on a dandelion in the yard. It teetered a bit like it had imbalance in its body (though bees do this a lot), soaked up some nectar, and then left. In ten seconds. I told my partner about it; her face lit up, as if the smallness of the moment was the whole point—which it is, really. That’s where meaning has to live now—tiny bursts upon the edges of attention. The bee didn’t know it was a bee; it didn’t know it was a marvel. It knew the flower’s sugar, the weight of its own wings going out of focus, the day too young for reputation. A poem could unfold from that moment, could name the bee’s fuzzy shoulder (or not), could let the dandelion be weed or flower depending on whether the reader had an upbringing that meant lawns. Meaning is parasitic on attention more than truth. We seed what we tend, and bees tend the future by tending the present—doing pollination not as a duty but as a compulsion of joy. The word “guest” fascinates me; it shares origin with “host,” the one who gives. We are all guests here on this shimmering planet, and the poorest hosts we can be is to leave it worse than we found it. So the bumblebee and the dandelion together are a parable: feed where you are, obscurely, with no demand for gratitude, and the field will pollenate into continuation. It’s not sentimental to believe this; it’s good engineering of life. The bee practises generosity without knowing the concept. That’s the kind of intelligence we might need.
